{{smaller block|<poem>Long were to tell
What I have done, what suffer’d; with what pain
''Voyaged'' the unreal, vast, unbounded deep.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., x. 471.}}
The Rhone of to-day must be something like the Rhine of fifty years ago, though much less ''voyaged'' now than that was then.

'''voyageable''' (voi′ạ̄j-ạ-bl), ''a.'' [< ''voyage'' + ''-able''.] Capable of being sailed or traveled over; navigable.

'''voyager''' (voi′ạ̄j-ėr), ''n.'' [< ''voyage'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who voyages; one who sails or passes by sea or water.
{{smaller block|You go on to prefer my Captivity in this Fleet to that of a ''Voyager'' at Sea.
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, ii. 39.}}
<poem>In a few short moments I retrace
(As in a map the ''voyager'' his course)
The windings of my way through many years.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, vi. 17.}}}}

'''voyageur''' (vwo-ya-zhėr′), ''n.'' [F., < ''voyager'', travel; as ''voyager''.] The Canadian name of one of a class of men employed by the Northwest and Hudson’s Bay companies in transporting men and supplies, and, in general, in keeping up communication between their various stations, which was done exclusively in bark canoes, the whole region formerly under the exclusive control of these companies being almost everywhere accessible by water, with few and short portages. These men were nearly always French Canadians or half-breeds.

'''vox''' (voks), ''n.''   [L.: see ''voice.'']   Voice; in ''music'', a voice or voice-part.—'''Vox angelica''', {{smaller|in ''organ-building'', a stop having two pipes to each digital, one of which is tuned slightly sharp, so that by their dissonance a wavy effect is produced. The pipes are of narrow scale, and the tone is delicate. Also ''vox cælestis, unda maris'', etc.}}—'''Vox antecedens''', {{smaller|the theme or antecedent of a canon or fugue.}}—'''Vox barbara''', {{smaller|a barbarous or outlandish word or phrase: commonly used, in zoölogy and botany, of those terms which are ostensibly New Latin, but which are neither Latin nor Greek, nor of classic derivation and formation, or are hybrids between Latin and Greek. Some thousands of such words are current, though rejected by some purists; and their use is far less objectionable than the unending confusion in nomenclature which attends the attempt to discard them. (See ''synonym'', 2 (''b'').) Usually abbreviated ''vox barb.''}}—'''Vox cælestis.''' {{smaller|Same as ''vox angelica.''}}—'''Vox consequens''', {{smaller|the answer or consequent of a canon or fugue.}}—'''Vox humana''', {{smaller|in ''organ-building'', a reed-stop having short capped pipes, so constructed as to reinforce the higher harmonics of the fundamental tones, and thus to produce tones more or less resembling those of the human voice. The imitation is not close, but under suitable conditions the illusion of a distant singer or choir is possible. The tremulant is usually combined with the vox humana. A stop of the same name, but of much less effectiveness, is often placed in reed-organs.}}—'''Vox quinta.''' {{smaller|Same as ''quintus.''}}

'''voyage''' (voi′āj), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''voiage''; < ME. ''voyage, voiage, veiage, veage, viage, vyage'', < OF. ''voiage, veiage, viage'', F. ''voyage'' = Sp. ''viaje'' = Pg. ''viagem'' = It. ''viaggio'', travel, journey, voyage, < L. ''viaticum'', provision for a journey, LL. a journey, neut. of ''viaticus'', pertaining to travel, ''via'', a way, road, journey, travel: see ''viaticum'', of which ''voyage'' is a doublet.]   '''1.''' Formerly, a passage or journey by land or by sea: now only a journey or passage by sea or water from one place, port, or country to another, especially a passing or journey by water to a distant place or country: as, a ''voyage'' to India.
{{smaller block|It is longe tyme passed that ther was no generalle Passage ne ''Vyage'' over the See; and many Men desiren for to here speke of the holy Lond, and han thereof gret Solace and Comfort. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Now to this lady lete vs turne ageyn,
Whiche to Surry hath take hir ''viage''.</poem>
{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 226.}}}}
{{smaller block|When I was determined to enter into my fourth ''voyage'', I cast into the ship, in the stead of merchandise, a pretty fardle of books.
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia (tr. by Robinson), ii. 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|Provyded also that no person or persons havinge chardge of any ''Viage'', in passinge from the Realme of Ireland or from the Isle of Manne into this Realme of England, do from the laste daye of June next comynge wittingly or wyllingly transporte . . . any Vacabond Roge or Beggar.
{{right|''Laws of'' 14 ''Eliz.'' (1572), quoted in Ribton-Turner’s}}
{{right|[Vagrants and Vagrancy, p. 109.}}}}
{{smaller block|The pasha was lately returned from his ''voyage'' towards Mecca, it being his office always to set out with provisions to meet the caravan in its return: they go about half way to Mecca, setting out the same day that the caravan usually leaves Mecca.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. i. 101.}}}}
{{smaller block|All being embarked, they bade farewell to the gazing throng upon the beach, who continued shouting after them, . . . wishing them a happy ''voyage''.
{{right|''Irving'', Knickerbocker, p. 110.}}}}
'''2.''' ''pl.'' A book of voyages: used like ''travels''.—'''3†.''' The practice of traveling. {{smaller block|Nations have interknowledge of one another by ''voyage'' into foreign parts. {{right|''Bacon.''}}}}
'''4†.''' A way or course taken; an attempt or undertaking; an enterprise; an expedition.
{{smaller block|<poem>And ek Diane! I the biseke
That this ''viage'' be noght to the loth.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 732.}}}}
{{smaller block|If you make your ''voyage'' upon her and give me directly to understand you have prevailed, I am no further your enemy. {{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, i. 4. 170.}}}}
{{smaller block|He ran away from me, . . . and pretended he would go the Island ''voyage'' [that against Hispaniola]; since, I ne’er heard of him till within this fortnight.
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|So great a dignitie in time past was not obteined to the maisters ther of by rebellion, . . . but by fighting valiauntly with the Moores in the ''voiage'' of Granado.

'''voyage''' (voi′āj), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''voyaged'', ppr. ''voyaging''.   [< OF. ''voyager'', travel, < ''voyage'', travel: see ''voyage''.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To take a journey or voyage; especially, to sail or pass by water.
{{smaller block|<poem>Beautiful bird! thou ''voyagest'' to thine home.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Alastor.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A mind for ever
''Voyaging'' through strange seas of Thought alone.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Prelude, iii.}}}}
'''II.''' ''trans.'' To travel; pass over; traverse.

<poem>Long were to tell
What I have done, what suffer’d; with what pain
''Voyaged'' the unreal, vast, unbounded deep.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Milton'', P. L., x. 471.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Rhone of to-day must be something like the Rhine of fifty years ago, though much less ''voyaged'' now than that was then.
{{right|''The Century'', XL. 636.}}}}

These men were nearly always French Canadians or half-breeds.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
